justification: Read against the live pages that actually cover this ground. TutorialsTeacher's interface page (a typical mid-ranking tutorial) never mentions the diamond problem, static abstract members, or an interfaces-vs-abstract-classes comparison at all — confirming the task's premise that most tutorials predate or ignore these C# 8/11 features. Microsoft's own 'fundamentals/types/interfaces' page gives the mnemonic-level comparison ('use an abstract class when related types share state...') with no code; its 'interface' keyword reference page and the static-virtual-interface-members tutorial cover the mechanics but with different examples (Point<T>/Translation<T>, RepeatSequence, IGetNext<T>) than this article's IAddable<TSelf>/Fraction and the diamond-collision Record/IPersistable/IAuditable/IEntity example — no shared running example, so no paraphrase risk. The diamond-problem section is the strongest original contribution: it correctly separates same-name-different-interface (no conflict, demonstrated) from a true shared-ancestor diamond (CS8705, demonstrated), quotes the C# language specification's §19.4.10 'most specific implementation' rule verbatim (I fetched standard/interfaces.md and diffed the quotes character-for-character: 'Every class and struct shall have a most specific implementation for every virtual member declared in all interfaces implemented by that type', 'an ambiguity arising from diamond interface inheritance', 'an error occurs' — all exact), and this level of treatment does not appear in any of the three comparison pages fetched. Fabrication check: all 6 front-matter sources are real, and I fetched all 6 directly. Five are cited inline; every inline quotation I checked (source 1: 'already released and used by innumerable clients'; source 6: the four spec quotes above) matches the live page verbatim and is used in the context the page supports. The MS-docs-correction claim is real and well-handled: the cited 'interface' keyword page ([2] in this article's own source list) currently states 'Interface members with a default implementation are private by default if you don't specify an access modifier' — which is wrong per the language specification's §19.4.1 ('All interface members implicitly have public access... with no special case for members that have a body') and is directly falsified by the article's own compiled code: SmsNotifier declares Describe with no modifier and no override, and calling it through an INotifier-typed variable from ordinary top-level code (i.e. from outside the interface) succeeds and prints output — if the member defaulted to private this call would fail exactly the way the later explicit-`private Log` example fails with CS0122. Crucially, the article never cites source [2] for the public-by-default claim; it cites [3] and [6] instead, so it never contradicts a source it is also relying on. This is a genuine, evidenced correction (spec quote + a compiled/run counter-demonstration), not an unfounded contradiction, and it is handled quietly and professionally rather than as a 'gotcha' callout. The static-abstract-members section stays narrow as the crosslinks file promises: one hand-built IAddable<TSelf>/Fraction example to show the mechanism, then one exercise that pivots to the real INumber<T> for the built-in numeric types, with no attempt at variance, erasure or the fuller constraint vocabulary — the crosslinks file's boundary note against the planned csharp-dotnet/generics article (CONTENT_PLAN §7.5 row 5, which also plans an INumber<T> sum) is accurate and genuinely useful coordination, not just a disclaimer. No filler intro/outro, no restated-title opening, no boilerplate Introduction/Conclusion/Key-takeaways headings; the closing section synthesizes (interface-segregation and composition-over-inheritance framing) rather than repeating headings. The toolchain sentence ('compiled and run with dotnet run on .NET 10.0.401, Windows 11, x64') sits once, right before the first code block, not as an opening sentence — compliant with the binding rule. Structure is genuinely varied against the only existing oop-design sibling, four-pillars-of-oop.md: that article is Q-shaped (10 of 16 headings are questions, per its own round-1 review); this article, assigned shape C in CONTENT_PLAN §7.4 row 4, uses mostly statement headings ('Default interface members: a method body...', 'Versioning: adding a member without breaking every implementer') with only two question-form H2s, and follows the planned outline (capabilities table → default members → state/constructors → versioning → decision guide) exactly. Five exercises use five different forms (predict-the-outcome, extend-the-code, explain-a-compile-failure, find-the-bug-in-a-diff, apply-the-decision-guide), spread through the article rather than bunched at the end, and none leaks its answer: predict-type questions show no output panel before the solution (the one code block tagged `error=CS0315` inside an exercise only surfaces the standard site-wide 'Does not compile' label, which states the given premise of the question, not the reasoning or BCL-interface answer being asked for). Two real defects keep this off a higher score. First, source [4] ('abstract keyword - C# reference', cited with an access date in front matter) is never cited inline anywhere in the body, despite covering claims the article makes without a citation — most notably 'Allowed, typically protected' for abstract-class constructors in the capabilities table, which is close to that very page's own sentence ('This constructor is typically protected, meaning only derived classes can access it'). This is exactly the failure mode the editorial brief's binding pilot-round lessons call a finding on its own. Second, the versioning section's line 'implementing an interface has always meant supplying every one of its members' is stated as an unscoped absolute, but the same section's next paragraph shows exactly the exception (a default body removes the obligation) — the claim is only true for members without a default and should say so rather than read as momentarily self-contradicted. Neither issue is a fabrication or a structural problem; both are sourcing/precision nits of the kind that keep strong articles at 'equal to Microsoft Learn quality with nits' rather than clearly ahead of it. `node tools/run-code.mjs` passes clean (PASS, blocks=31, executed=20, matching the expected count) with every quoted diagnostic (CS0525, CS0526, CS0122, CS1061, CS8705, CS0535, CS0315) verified against the actual compiler by the harness, not asserted by the writer. Render-level checks (console errors, broken links, Lighthouse, screenshots) were not run this round and are left to the design/UX critic's pass.
